section.title: Israel Oppressed in Egypt
section.sectionRationale: The book opens with a short roll call that hooks Exodus to Genesis, then a rapid time jump: a new king arises, and the seam of the whole book turns on his fear. Two scenes carry the chapter: Pharaoh's policy of crushing labor, and his failed plot through the midwives.
section.thesis: The God who filled the earth through Abraham's family is still multiplying His people even as a frightened empire tries to grind them down, and the fear of God in two lowly midwives outlasts the fear of a king.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: the seed of Jacob multiplies in Egypt; a new king enslaves them with forced labor; the king's plot to kill the sons fails before the courage of Shiphrah and Puah.

units.label: A people multiplying
units.note: the promise to Abraham is being kept

verses.text: These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob, each with his family:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah;
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin;
Dan and Naphtali; Gad and Asher.
The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all, including Joseph, who was already in Egypt.
Now Joseph and all his brothers and all that generation died,
but the Israelites were {{parah|fruitful}} and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them.

units.label: A new king, a crushing labor

verses.text: Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt.
“Look,” he said to his people, “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more; and if a war breaks out, they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.”
So the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. As a result, they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh.
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished; so the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.
They worked the Israelites ruthlessly
and made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields. Every service they imposed was harsh.

units.label: The midwives fear God
units.note: a plot against the sons fails

verses.text: Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, whose names were Shiphrah and Puah,
“When you help the Hebrew women give birth, observe them on the birthstools. If the child is a son, kill him; but if it is a daughter, let her live.”
The midwives, however, {{yare|feared God}} and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live.
So the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and asked them, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?”
The midwives answered Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives.”
So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous.
And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own.
Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, “You must throw every son born to the Hebrews into the Nile, but let every daughter live.”

parah.gloss: To be fruitful. The same word used of the creation blessing in Genesis 1:28 and the promise to Abraham in Genesis 17:6. Under Pharaoh's boot, God's creation and covenant blessing is still quietly at work.

yare.gloss: To fear or revere. The midwives fear God rather than the king, the same word used for the fear of the LORD that is the beginning of wisdom, Proverbs 9:10. Their fear of God overrules their fear of Pharaoh.

basic.context: Exodus opens where Genesis left off: Jacob's family went down to Egypt seventy strong. Centuries pass, they multiply into a nation, and a new Pharaoh who does not remember Joseph turns them into slaves. Even so, God keeps multiplying them, and two brave midwives refuse to kill the baby boys.
basic.hermeneutics: This is straightforward historical narrative describing real events. It is not telling us to disobey every government, but it does show that when a ruler commands what God forbids, faithful people must obey God rather than man, as Shiphrah and Puah did.
basic.originalLanguages: The Israelites are fruitful, parah, the very word for the blessing of creation and of Abraham's covenant. The midwives feared God, yare, the same fear that is the beginning of wisdom. Their fear of God is stronger than their fear of Pharaoh's throne.
basic.typology: Pharaoh's order to drown the sons anticipates Herod's slaughter of the infants in Matthew 2, another tyrant trying to kill the deliverer God is raising up. Both fail, and both point to a hostility toward God's rescuing work that the New Testament traces back to the serpent.
basic.christ: The chapter sets the stage for Israel's exodus, the great Old Testament picture of redemption that Christ Himself fulfills, delivering His people not from Egypt but from sin and death. The attempt to kill Israel's sons foreshadows Herod's attempt on the infant Jesus, the true and greater deliverer.
basic.god: God is quietly sovereign here; His name is not even mentioned until verse 17, yet He is behind the multiplying of His people and behind the courage of two ordinary women. He rewards those who fear Him above earthly power.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 46 lists this same family going to Egypt. Acts 7 retells this history in Stephen's speech. Matthew 2 echoes Pharaoh's plot in Herod's slaughter of the innocents.
basic.oneStory: This is the hinge between the patriarchs and the exodus. A small family becomes an enslaved nation, and God is already at work to deliver them, using the courage of two women who fear Him more than Pharaoh. The rescue that follows becomes the pattern for every rescue God works after it, culminating in Christ.

context.literary:
Exodus opens with the word 'and' in Hebrew, 'And these are the names,' so that the book presents itself as the continuation of Genesis rather than a new beginning. Verses 1 to 5 repeat, in compressed form, the family list of Genesis 46:8-27, and verse 6 echoes Genesis 50:26: Joseph dies, and with him 'all that generation.' The seventy who went down are named; the multitude that follows is not. A family has become a people.

The chapter then moves in three rising waves, each an attempt by Pharaoh to stop Israel's growth, and each failing. First comes forced labour, verses 8 to 14: 'the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied,' verse 12. Second comes a secret order to the midwives, verses 15 to 21, which is defeated by two women who fear God. Third comes a public decree to the whole nation, verse 22, to throw every newborn son into the Nile. The pressure escalates from hard work to hidden murder to open genocide. Each stage is answered by a notice that the people 'multiplied,' verses 7, 12 and 20, until the chapter ends on the decree with no answer yet. The answer comes in chapter 2, in a single baby placed in the very river meant to kill him.

The narrative pace is striking. Centuries pass between verses 6 and 8 in a single sentence, and then the story slows to a conversation between a king and two midwives. The narrator names the midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, but never names the Pharaoh. The most powerful man in the world is simply 'the king of Egypt,' while the two women who defy him are remembered by name.

The chapter also sets up the book's great theme through a single word. The root avad, 'to work, to serve,' runs again and again through verses 13 and 14, describing Israel's slavery. The rest of Exodus will turn the same word around: God demands, 'let My son go so that he may worship Me,' Exodus 4:23, using the same verb. The question of the book is whom Israel will serve.
context.historical:
The setting is the eastern Nile Delta, the region Genesis calls Goshen and 'the district of Rameses,' Genesis 47:11. Pithom and Rameses, verse 11, were 'store cities,' supply centres for grain and military stores on the approach to Egypt from the east. The name Rameses is associated with the kings of that name in Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, and its use has shaped the debate about when these events happened. Forced labour on royal building projects, including brick making, is well attested in ancient Egypt, and Egyptian mud brick was made from Nile silt mixed with straw, as Exodus 5:7 assumes.

The change of regime in verse 8, 'a new king, who did not know Joseph,' implies more than a new ruler. It suggests a change of dynasty or policy in which the old debt to Joseph no longer counted. Pharaoh's fear, verse 10, is strategic: the eastern Delta was Egypt's exposed frontier, and a large foreign population there might side with invaders. His plan to 'deal shrewdly' is the reasoning of state security, which makes the cruelty that follows all the more chilling.

The midwives are called 'Hebrew midwives,' and 'Hebrew' is the term foreigners typically used for Abraham's descendants, as in 'Abram the Hebrew,' Genesis 14:13. Two named women were probably leaders over a larger group of midwives rather than the only two for the whole people. The 'birthstools' of verse 16 were the stones or stool on which women crouched to give birth.

The BSB footnote on verse 5 notes that the Hebrew text reads seventy, while the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek Septuagint read seventy-five, the number Stephen uses in Acts 7:14. The difference comes from whether Joseph's grandsons are counted, and it shows Stephen following the Greek Bible of his hearers.
context.canonical:
The chapter's first move is to show a promise being kept. Verse 7 piles up the vocabulary of Genesis 1:28, 'be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth,' and of God's promise to Abraham, 'I will multiply you exceedingly,' Genesis 17:2. Deuteronomy 10:22 later sums up the result: 'Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars in the sky.' The oppression itself was foretold: Abraham's descendants would be 'strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years,' Genesis 15:13.

Israel never forgot the slavery. The confession at the offering of firstfruits recited, 'the Egyptians mistreated us and afflicted us, putting us to hard labor,' Deuteronomy 26:6. The law applied the memory directly: the word 'ruthlessly' in verses 13 and 14 returns in Leviticus 25:43 and 25:46, which forbid Israelites to 'rule harshly' over a fellow Israelite. What Egypt did to them, they must never do to one another. Psalm 105:24-25 retells the chapter with a startling perspective: the LORD 'made His people very fruitful' and turned the Egyptians' hearts 'to hate His people.'

The prophets use Pharaoh as a type of arrogant power. Ezekiel 29:3 addresses him as the 'great monster who lies among his rivers,' who says 'The Nile is mine.' The river Pharaoh made an instrument of death is pictured as his own lair.

In the New Testament Stephen retells the chapter in Acts 7:17-19, noting that the people increased 'as the time drew near for God to fulfill His promise to Abraham,' and that the king forced them 'to abandon their infants.' Matthew's account of Herod's slaughter in Bethlehem, Matthew 2:16, follows the same pattern, and Revelation 12:4-5 gathers every such attempt into one picture: a dragon waiting before a woman in labour, ready to devour her child.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote this chapter for a people who had come out of Egypt, and he wanted them to understand three things about their own beginnings.

First, that their very existence as a nation was the fulfilment of God's word. The piling up of words for growth in verse 7 is meant to make them hear Genesis. They were not an accident of demography; they were the promised seed of Abraham, multiplying as God said they would.

Second, that their suffering was real and was seen. The chapter does not hurry past the bitterness of the labour or the horror of the decree. It names the cruelty for what it was, and it makes clear that the conflict was never merely between Egypt and Israel. A king who set himself against the promise was setting himself against God, and the plagues and the sea will show who is stronger.

Third, that God's victory begins in small, faithful acts. Before there is a burning bush, a staff or a plague, there are two women who will not kill babies. The first act of resistance in Exodus is the fear of God in ordinary people. Moses wanted Israel to see that the same God who would split the sea also honoured the quiet courage of midwives, and that every Israelite could share in His purposes by fearing Him more than any king.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes events; it does not lay down laws. Pharaoh's policies are recorded to be condemned, and later law explicitly forbids an Israelite to treat a fellow Israelite the way Egypt treated them, Leviticus 25:43. The midwives' refusal to kill is commended, since God 'was good to the midwives,' verse 20, but the text does not turn their method into a rule.

What carries forward is the principle that some commands of human authority must be refused. The apostles state it directly, 'We must obey God rather than men,' Acts 5:29, and Daniel and his friends lived it. The midwives' case is especially clear because the command was to take innocent life. Believers today face their own versions of this question, and the chapter shows that the fear of God, not the fear of consequences, is what makes such refusal possible, Proverbs 29:25. The narrative also encourages patience. God's answer to the oppression is not immediate, and the chapter closes on an unanswered decree, reminding believers that God's timing is not always quick even when His purpose is sure.

debates.question: Were the midwives right to deceive Pharaoh?

views.label: Their fear of God is commended, not the deception
views.case: Verses 17 and 21 credit their fearing God and letting the boys live. The text never explicitly praises their words to Pharaoh, and the ninth commandment, Exodus 20:16, forbids false witness. On this view God blessed their courage and faithfulness in spite of an imperfect answer, much as Rahab is commended for welcoming the spies, James 2:25, rather than for her words at the door. This was Augustine's view.

views.label: Deceiving a murderer is not wrongful lying
views.case: Others argue that the command against false witness concerns one's neighbour in matters of justice, and that a tyrant seeking to kill the innocent has forfeited any right to the truth. God rewards the midwives immediately after their answer, verses 20 and 21, and elsewhere tells Samuel to give a partial account to avoid Saul's violence, 1 Samuel 16:2. Many later interpreters have argued along these lines.

views.label: Their answer may have been true
views.case: A few suggest the midwives' answer contained real truth, that Hebrew women often did give birth quickly, and that the midwives deliberately arrived late. On this reading they deceived by omission rather than outright falsehood.

debates.bearing: The passage clearly commends refusing to take part in murder even at great risk, and it roots that courage in the fear of God. It leaves room for careful reflection on how believers speak to those bent on evil, without making deception itself the point.

debates.question: When did the oppression and the exodus take place?

views.label: An earlier date, around the fifteenth century BC
views.case: 1 Kings 6:1 places the exodus 480 years before Solomon began the temple, which points to the mid fifteenth century BC. On this view the 'new king' of verse 8 may belong to the dynasty that drove out foreign rulers from the Delta, and the name Rameses in verse 11 is an updated place name, as it is already in Genesis 47:11 for Joseph's time.

views.label: A later date, in the thirteenth century BC
views.case: The store city Rameses is naturally connected with Rameses II, a great builder in the eastern Delta. On this view the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 is a symbolic figure, twelve generations of forty years, and the oppression belongs to the Nineteenth Dynasty.

debates.bearing: Faithful scholars hold both views, and the evidence is complex. The theology of the chapter does not depend on the date: a real people were really enslaved, and God really delivered them. What matters most is the question Pharaoh himself will ask, 'Who is the LORD?', Exodus 5:2.

debates.question: Were Shiphrah and Puah Hebrews or Egyptians?

views.label: Hebrew women
views.case: The most natural reading of the phrase is 'Hebrew midwives,' and their names are Semitic. Their fear of God fits women who belonged to the covenant people, and God giving them 'families of their own,' verse 21, may mean their households became part of Israel's future.

views.label: Egyptian midwives to the Hebrews
views.case: The Hebrew can also be read 'the midwives of the Hebrews,' and some ancient Jewish interpreters, Josephus among them, took them as Egyptians. It would seem odd for Pharaoh to trust Hebrew women to kill Hebrew babies. On this reading the chapter shows Gentiles fearing God, as Pharaoh's own daughter will show compassion in chapter 2.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the question, and either way the point stands: the fear of God, not ethnicity, is what made these women heroines. If they were Egyptians, the chapter anticipates the 'mixed multitude' who left Egypt, Exodus 12:38, with Israel and the nations who will one day fear the LORD.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 7 is a small anthology of creation language. It uses five verbs and phrases of increase in a row: 'were fruitful,' 'increased rapidly,' 'multiplied,' 'became exceedingly numerous,' and 'the land was filled.' The second, sharats, is literally 'swarmed' or 'teemed,' the verb used of the waters that 'teem with living creatures' in Genesis 1:20-21. The phrase 'exceedingly,' bim'od me'od, is the doubled intensive of God's promise to Abram, 'I will multiply you exceedingly,' Genesis 17:2. The narrator wants Israel's growth heard as the blessing of creation and covenant coming true.

Pharaoh's proposal in verse 10, 'let us deal shrewdly with them,' uses the verb chakam, 'to be wise,' in a reflexive form, 'let us act wisely.' The irony is deliberate: Egypt's worldly wisdom is set against the midwives' fear of God. His opening 'Come,' havah, is the same word the builders of Babel used, 'Come, let us make bricks,' Genesis 11:3, and Egypt too builds with brick in defiance of God.

Verse 12 says the Egyptians 'came to dread' the Israelites. The verb quts means to feel loathing mixed with fear. Numbers 22:3 uses it when 'Moab dreaded the Israelites,' also because they were numerous. The empire that thought it could control Israel ends up afraid of them.

The word 'ruthlessly' in verses 13 and 14, perek, means harsh, crushing severity. It returns in Leviticus 25:43, 46 and 53, where Israel is forbidden to rule over a fellow Israelite 'harshly,' and in Ezekiel 34:4, of shepherds who 'ruled them with violence and cruelty.' The law remembered Egypt's word and forbade it.

Those verses also make the Israelites' lives 'bitter,' from marar, the root of the 'bitter herbs,' merorim, eaten at the Passover, Exodus 12:8. Every Passover meal would taste the bitterness of this chapter.

The 'birthstools' of verse 16, ovnayim, is a dual form built on the word for stone, 'the two stones.' The same word describes the potter's 'wheel' in Jeremiah 18:3. It probably refers to stones or a stool on which a woman crouched in labour.

Finally, verse 21 says that God 'gave them families of their own,' literally 'made houses for them.' The word bayit means house, household and dynasty. Pharaoh forced Israel to build him cities; God builds houses for the midwives. The same language appears when the LORD promises David that 'He Himself will establish a house for you,' 2 Samuel 7:11. The God who builds households is the true builder, Psalm 127:1.

typology.type: Slavery in Egypt, the pattern of bondage to sin
typology.fulfillment: Israel's forced service to Pharaoh, hard, bitter and inescapable, becomes in the New Testament a picture of humanity's bondage to sin. 'Everyone who sins is a slave to sin,' Jesus says, and 'if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed,' John 8:34-36. Paul describes believers as those who 'once were slaves to sin' but have been 'set free,' Romans 6:17-18. The escalation is that the new exodus frees not from a human king but from sin and death, Hebrews 2:14-15. The type falls short because Israel's slavery was imposed from outside, while bondage to sin is also a slavery we choose, from which only God can free us.

typology.type: The king who sets himself against the promised children
typology.fulfillment: Pharaoh's decree to kill the newborn sons is the first great attempt in Scripture to destroy the people of promise at its source. Herod's order to kill the boys of Bethlehem, Matthew 2:16, repeats the pattern, and in both cases the child God has chosen survives. Revelation 12:4-5 unveils the power behind every such attempt: a dragon waiting 'to devour her child as soon as she gave birth.' The pattern goes back to the enmity of Genesis 3:15. The escalation in Christ is that the child who escapes goes on to defeat the dragon itself, 'caught up to God and to His throne,' and will rule all nations.

typology.type: The people who multiply under pressure
typology.fulfillment: Egypt's oppression only made Israel grow, verse 12. The early church saw the same pattern in its own life. When persecution scattered the believers from Jerusalem, 'those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went,' Acts 8:4. When Herod killed James and imprisoned Peter, and then died under God's judgment, Luke adds, 'But the word of God continued to spread and multiply,' Acts 12:24. The correspondence is not automatic, for persecution does sometimes destroy churches, but it shows the same God at work, turning the enemy's pressure into growth. The escalation is that the church multiplies not by births alone but by new birth, as the gospel spreads to the nations.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by setting the stage for the exodus, the Old Testament's great act of redemption. The New Testament uses exodus language for the work of Jesus. Luke calls His coming death His 'departure,' literally His exodus, Luke 9:31. Paul calls Christ 'our Passover lamb,' 1 Corinthians 5:7. Zechariah praises God for raising up a Saviour to grant 'deliverance from hostile hands, that we may serve Him without fear,' Luke 1:74, which is the exodus described in personal terms. Without the bondage of Exodus 1 there would be no exodus, and without the language of that exodus the New Testament would not have the vocabulary it uses to describe redemption.

It leads to Christ by pattern. The attempt to kill Israel's sons is repeated when Herod tries to kill Jesus. Matthew shapes his account so that the infant Jesus relives Israel's story: a king's slaughter of boys, a flight to Egypt, and a return, 'Out of Egypt I called My Son,' Matthew 2:15. Jesus is the true Israel, the Son whom God protects and calls out.

It leads to Christ by the theme of service. The chapter's key word, avad, describes Israel's slavery to Pharaoh, and God's demand to Pharaoh is 'let My son go so that he may worship Me,' using the same word, Exodus 4:23. The exodus exchanges one service for another. Jesus came 'not to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. He took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, entering human bondage in order to set His people free for the glad service of God.

It leads to Christ by contrast. Pharaoh built cities by the forced labour of the oppressed and tried to secure his rule by killing children. Christ builds His house by laying down His life, and He welcomes children, 'Let the little children come to Me,' Matthew 19:14. Pharaoh's 'wisdom' in verse 10 is the wisdom of the world that God makes foolish at the cross, 1 Corinthians 1:20-25.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The midwives are not pictures of Christ, and Pithom and Rameses are not symbols. The chapter leads to Christ through the shape of the larger story it begins, and through the New Testament's own use of the exodus to describe what He has done.
study.god:
The chapter shows first that God keeps His word across time. Centuries pass between Genesis and verse 8, and yet the promise to Abraham, 'I will multiply you exceedingly,' Genesis 17:2, is visibly being fulfilled. God does not need to appear in a vision to be at work. His promise itself is active, and the growth of the people is its evidence.

He is sovereign over the powers of the world. Pharaoh is the most powerful ruler of his day, and he uses every tool at his disposal, economic, secret and public. None of it works. The more he oppresses, the more Israel multiplies, verse 12. Psalm 105:25 goes further and says God turned the Egyptians' hearts to hate His people. God's sovereignty reaches even into the hostility of His enemies, not to excuse their cruelty but to ensure it serves His purpose.

He is known in this chapter only as 'God,' Elohim. The covenant name, the LORD, will not appear until the burning bush in Exodus 3. Yet the God who is barely named is the one who decides the outcome. His absence from the first sixteen verses is a narrative silence, not a real absence, and it mirrors how the oppressed often experience Him: hidden, but not gone.

He honours those who fear Him. The midwives feared God, verse 17, and God 'was good to the midwives,' verse 20, and 'gave them families,' verse 21. The one who sees what happens in the birthing rooms of slaves is the same God who judges kings. The fear of God is not terror of an unpredictable power but reverent trust in the one who is truly in control, and it frees the midwives from the fear of Pharaoh. 'The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him,' Psalm 34:7.

He is the God of life against the powers of death. Pharaoh's policy moves toward killing, and God's work moves toward life, multiplying, preserving and building houses. The Nile, which Pharaoh intends as a grave for Hebrew boys, will become the place where God preserves the deliverer, and later the sea where Pharaoh's own army drowns, Exodus 15:4. God's justice often turns the weapon of the wicked back upon them.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to trust God's promises when He seems silent, to fear Him more than any earthly power, and to take courage that even small acts of faithfulness are seen and honoured by Him.

crossReferences.note: God's first blessing, 'be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth.' Exodus 1:7 uses the same verbs for Israel, so their growth in Egypt is heard as the creation blessing working through the chosen family, even in a foreign land.

God told Abram that his descendants would be 'strangers in a land that is not their own' and would be 'enslaved and mistreated four hundred years,' but that He would judge the nation they served. Exodus 1 is the beginning of that foretold oppression.

Joseph's dying words, 'God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land.' Exodus 1 opens after his death and the death of his generation, and the new king's ignorance of Joseph sets the scene for that promised visit.

The confession Israel recited at the offering of firstfruits: 'the Egyptians mistreated us and afflicted us, putting us to hard labor,' and the LORD 'brought us out.' Exodus 1 became part of Israel's regular worship and memory.

The law forbids Israelites to rule over a fellow Israelite 'harshly,' using the same word as the 'ruthless' labour of Exodus 1:13-14. Israel's own experience of oppression was meant to shape how they treated those who worked for them.

The psalmist retells the chapter from God's side: the LORD made His people 'very fruitful, more numerous than their foes,' and turned the Egyptians' hearts 'to hate His people.' It shows the divine sovereignty operating even in the enemy's hostility.

Stephen's summary of the chapter. The people 'increased greatly' as the time drew near for God to fulfil His promise, and the king 'exploited our people,' forcing them 'to abandon their infants.' Stephen uses the story to show God keeping His promise despite opposition.

The apostles, ordered to stop preaching, reply, 'We must obey God rather than men.' The midwives lived by this principle long before it was spoken, refusing a royal command that required them to kill.

Herod's slaughter of the boys of Bethlehem repeats Pharaoh's decree. In both cases a king tries to kill a promised child by killing all the children, and in both cases God preserves the one He has chosen.

The dragon stands before the woman 'ready to devour her child as soon as she gave birth.' John reveals the enemy behind every attempt to destroy God's people at its source, including Pharaoh's, and the child's victory.
Moses' parents hid him, 'unafraid of the king's edict.' The decree of Exodus 1:22 is the edict in view, and the fear of God shown by the midwives is carried forward into the faith of Moses' parents.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God blessed humanity, 'be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth,' Genesis 1:28. After the fall that blessing continued, but in a world where death and violence were always pressing against it. God chose Abraham's family to carry the blessing to all nations, Genesis 12:3, promising descendants as numerous as the stars. Exodus 1 shows that promise coming true in a hostile place, and it shows the old enmity of Genesis 3:15 flaring up against it. A king sets himself against the growth God is giving, and the war between the serpent and the woman's seed takes the form of an empire against a people of slaves.

The chapter answers what Genesis left open. Genesis ended with a family in Egypt and a promise that God would visit them, Genesis 50:24. Exodus 1 explains why they need to be visited: the land that once saved them now enslaves them. It also explains how a family of seventy could become a nation able to inherit the land.

It sets up everything that follows. The slavery of Exodus 1 is the backdrop for the whole exodus, the plagues, the Passover, the crossing of the sea and the covenant at Sinai. The question of whom Israel will serve, Pharaoh or the LORD, drives the book to its end, where God comes to dwell among the people who once built store cities for a king.

The story comes to rest in Christ. The exodus becomes the pattern for every later rescue, and the prophets promise a new exodus from exile. Jesus enacts it. He is the Son called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15. He accomplishes His exodus at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31. He frees people from the slavery of sin, John 8:36, and makes them servants of God, Romans 6:18.

The new creation completes what this chapter begins. The church, like Israel in Egypt, often grows under pressure, and one day the multitude will be 'too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9. The blessing of Genesis 1:28, threatened by every Pharaoh, will fill the earth. There will be no more oppressors and no more bitter labour. God's people will serve Him freely, 'and His servants will worship Him,' Revelation 22:3.

quiz.q: Why did the new king of Egypt turn against the Israelites?

options.text: The Israelites asked to be enslaved.
options.note: Nothing in the text suggests this; the oppression is imposed against their will.

options.text: God commanded Pharaoh to oppress them as judgment.
options.note: This reverses the text; God is not the source of the oppression, Pharaoh's fear is.

options.text: They had committed a crime against Egypt.
options.note: The text gives no such accusation; it is fear of numbers and power, not any wrongdoing.

options.text: He feared their growing numbers and strength and wanted to control them.
options.note: Verses 9 to 10 give his own stated fear as the reason for the oppression.

quiz.q: What happened despite Pharaoh's forced labor?

options.text: They stopped having children in protest.
options.note: Not in the text; it records growth despite hardship.

options.text: Their numbers slowly declined.
options.note: The opposite is true; oppression did not stop their growth.

options.text: They were completely wiped out.
options.note: The chapter shows survival and multiplication, not destruction.

options.text: The Israelites multiplied and flourished all the more.
options.note: Verse 12 says the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied.

quiz.q: Why did Shiphrah and Puah refuse to kill the newborn sons?

options.text: They were afraid of being caught by other Hebrews.
options.note: The stated reason is fear of God, not fear of their own people.

options.text: They had no opinion either way.
options.note: Their fear of God is the explicit, deliberate motive given in the text.

options.text: They feared God more than they feared Pharaoh.
options.note: Verse 17 states plainly that the midwives feared God.

options.text: They did not understand Pharaoh's command.
options.note: They understood it clearly and chose not to obey it.

quiz.q: How did God respond to the midwives' courage?

options.text: He punished them for deceiving Pharaoh.
options.note: The text records reward, not punishment, for their fear of God.

options.text: He was good to them and gave them families of their own.
options.note: Verses 20 to 21 record God's kindness to them because they feared Him.

options.text: He ignored them entirely.
options.note: God's attention to them is explicit in the text.

options.text: He made them queens of Egypt.
options.note: This is not in the text; their reward was families, not political power.

quiz.q: What does this chapter show about God's covenant promise to Abraham?

options.text: It has nothing to do with this chapter.
options.note: The fruitfulness language directly recalls the Abrahamic promise.

options.text: It had failed because of the slavery.
options.note: The opposite is shown; the promise advances precisely through the hardship.

options.text: It was still being fulfilled even under brutal oppression.
options.note: The Israelites' fruitfulness echoes the promise of Genesis 15 and 17, advancing despite Pharaoh's plans.

options.text: It was replaced by a new promise to Pharaoh.
options.note: Nothing in the text suggests any promise to Pharaoh; the covenant is with Abraham's descendants.

questions: The Israelites flourished even under crushing oppression. Where do you need to trust that God's purposes are still advancing even when your circumstances feel like Pharaoh's brickyards?
Shiphrah and Puah risked their lives because they feared God more than the king. Where is fearing people, rather than fearing God, shaping your choices right now?
Pharaoh's cruelty could not stop the fulfillment of God's promise. What situation in your life feels immovable, and how does this chapter reframe what God can do in it?
God rewarded two ordinary midwives whose names history almost forgot. How does it encourage you that God notices small, costly acts of faithfulness that no one else may ever applaud?
The chapter closes with Pharaoh's most brutal order yet, and still God is at work. Where do you need hope that the darkest verse is never God's last word?

translationNotes.note: The Masoretic Text has seventy descendants, matching Genesis 46:27, while the Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek Septuagint, followed in Acts 7:14, have seventy five, likely counting additional grandsons of Joseph.
The phrase rendered leave the country can also be translated take the country, changing whether Pharaoh fears the Israelites fleeing or seizing power.
Some ancient versions add to the Hebrews to Pharaoh's final command, specifying the sons in view, though the Hebrew text itself does not include that phrase.
